items: Saint Luke is traditionally remembered as a physician and companion of Saint Paul.
The word 'Gospel' comes from an Old English word meaning 'good news'; the Greek term is euangelion.
The Catholic Bible contains 73 books: 46 in the Old Testament and 27 in the New Testament.
The Psalms are prayers and songs that include praise, thanksgiving, lament and trust.
The word 'Alleluia' comes from Hebrew words meaning 'Praise the Lord'.
Advent begins the Church's liturgical year in the Roman Rite.
The Easter season lasts fifty days and concludes with Pentecost.
The word 'Eucharist' comes from a Greek word meaning thanksgiving.
The Beatitudes are found in Matthew 5 and Luke 6, with different arrangements and wording.
Saint Jerome is especially associated with the Latin Bible known as the Vulgate.
The Acts of the Apostles describes the early Church and the spread of the Gospel after the Resurrection.
The Magnificat is Mary's song of praise in Luke 1:46–55.
Bethlehem is associated with the birth of Jesus and with King David's family.
The word 'Messiah' and the word 'Christ' both mean 'Anointed One' in their respective language traditions.
The Rosary meditates on events in the lives of Jesus and Mary through Scripture-rooted mysteries.
The liturgical colour violet is commonly used in Advent and Lent as a sign of preparation and penance.
Pentecost commemorates the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the disciples.
Saint Mark's traditional symbol is a winged lion.
Saint Luke's traditional symbol is a winged ox.
The word 'Amen' expresses affirmation and trust, often understood as 'so be it' or 'truly'.
